lead.t: They are broadly classified into Hodgkin lymphoma (HL) and non‑Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) based on histopathology and immunophenotype.

b: Classification uses cell lineage, stage of differentiation, morphology, immunophenotype, genetics and clinical behaviour .

B-cell neoplasms (85-90%): diffuse large B-cell (DLBCL, the commonest, about a third), follicular, CLL/SLL, mantle cell, marginal zone/MALT, Burkitt, lymphoplasmacytic, hairy cell leukaemia, plasma cell myeloma.

T/NK-cell neoplasms (10-15%): peripheral T-cell lymphoma, anaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALCL), mycosis fungoides/Sezary syndrome, adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma (HTLV-1), NK/T-cell lymphoma (nasal type, EBV).
Precursor tumours: B- and T-lymphoblastic leukaemia/lymphoma, in children and adolescents.

qs.q: What is the most common subtype of B-cell Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma (NHL)?
qs.e: Diffuse Large B-cell Lymphoma (DLBCL) is the most common subtype of B-cell Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma, accounting for approximately 30-40% of all NHLs. It is an aggressive lymphoma but often curable.
qs.s: Weekly Pathology Exam - October 16, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: What percentage of Non-Hodgkin Lymphomas are of B-cell origin?
qs.e: NHL is 85% B-cell and 15% T/NK-cell origin. This is a foundational fact frequently tested.

qs.q: What is the incidence of Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma per 100,000 population?
qs.e: The incidence of NHL is approximately 15-20 per 100,000, making it significantly more common than Hodgkin lymphoma.
qs.s: Weekly Pathology Exam - March 7, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

es.q: A 68-year-old male presents with new-onset, painless cervical lymphadenopathy. Biopsy confirms Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma (NHL). Briefly outline the primary cellular origins of NHL and their approximate percentages.
es.m: Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma is a diverse group of clonal lymphoid tumors. Approximately 85% are of B-cell origin, while 15% arise from T or NK cells.
es.s: Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma: Classification, Symptoms, Diagnosis, and Treatment — Pract

es.q: Differentiate between low-grade (indolent) and high-grade (aggressive) Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma in terms of their typical disease course, curability, and urgency of treatment.
es.m: Low-grade (indolent) NHLs are slow-growing, difficult to cure, and often allow for a 'watch and wait' approach. High-grade (aggressive) NHLs are rapidly progressive, more often curable, and require urgent treatment.
es.s: Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma: Classification, Symptoms, Diagnosis, and Treatment — Pract

es.q: Describe the gold standard diagnostic investigation for Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma (NHL) and explain why Fine Needle Aspiration (FNA) is generally considered insufficient.
es.m: The gold standard diagnostic investigation for NHL is a trucut or whole lymph node biopsy. Fine Needle Aspiration (FNA) is insufficient because it typically does not provide adequate tissue architecture necessary for definitive classification and subtyping of NHL.
es.s: Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma: Classification, Symptoms, Diagnosis, and Treatment — Pract

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) is a heterogeneous group of clonal lymphoid cancers, most often B‑cell origin, that spread non‑contiguously. Diagnosis relies on morphology, immunophenotype and genetics; treatment uses chemo‑immunotherapy.

sections.p: NHL comprises clonal proliferations of lymphocytes that lack Reed‑Sternberg cells. Diagnosis requires tissue biopsy showing atypical lymphoid cells, immunophenotyping (CD20 for B‑cells), and often a defining genetic abnormality such as t(14;18) in follicular lymphoma.
b: Biopsy with histology and immunohistochemistry is mandatory
Genetic testing (FISH, PCR) confirms specific subtypes

t.b: Confirms lymphoma type and grade; morphology plus CD20 positivity indicates B‑cell NHL
Identifies cell surface markers; CD20+ CD5‑ suggests most B‑cell NHL, guiding therapy
Detects BCL2 translocation; positive result supports follicular lymphoma diagnosis

sections.p: The Ann Arbor system (modified for NHL) stages disease from I (single region) to IV (disseminated). The International Prognostic Index (IPI) adds age, LDH, performance status, stage and extranodal sites to predict outcome.
b: Stage I–II: limited disease, often curable
Stage III–IV: advanced, need systemic therapy
High IPI score predicts poorer survival

sections.p: Most NHL cases are idiopathic, but risk factors include immunodeficiency (HIV, organ transplant), chronic infections (H. pylori, EBV, hepatitis C), and autoimmune diseases.
b: HIV infection markedly increases aggressive B‑cell NHL
H. pylori gastritis can trigger gastric MALT lymphoma
Chronic hepatitis C linked to splenic marginal zone lymphoma

sections.p: Patients often notice painless lymphadenopathy, sometimes with B symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss). Extranodal disease may cause organ‑specific symptoms, e.g., abdominal mass or testicular swelling in older men.
b: Painless, progressive lymph node enlargement
Constitutional B symptoms in 30% of aggressive NHL
Extranodal sites: GI tract, CNS, testis

sections.p: Beyond tissue diagnosis, staging uses imaging and laboratory studies to assess disease burden and organ function before therapy.
b: CT or PET‑CT maps nodal and extranodal disease
Baseline labs evaluate marrow involvement and treatment safety

t.b: Determines metabolic activity and stage; high uptake indicates active disease and guides radiotherapy fields
Detects marrow infiltration; positive result upstages to IV and influences prognosis
Elevated LDH reflects high tumor turnover; part of IPI scoring
Identifies immunodeficiency that alters treatment choice and prognosis

sections.p: Rapidly enlarging nodes, new organ dysfunction, or severe B symptoms suggest aggressive disease needing urgent therapy. Tumor lysis syndrome, infections, and treatment‑related cytopenias are common complications.
b: Sudden node growth → possible transformation to high‑grade lymphoma
Renal failure from tumor lysis
Severe neutropenia → opportunistic infection

sections.p: First‑line therapy combines chemotherapy (e.g., CHOP) with anti‑CD20 monoclonal antibody rituximab for CD20‑positive B‑cell NHL. Radiotherapy is added for localized disease. Supportive care includes growth‑factor support and infection prophylaxis.
b: Rituximab targets CD20, depletes B‑cells, improves survival
Avoid anthracycline in cardiac disease; consider bendamustine as alternative
Treat underlying infections (e.g., H. pylori eradication) before chemo

sections.p: After remission, patients are monitored with periodic physical exam, imaging, and labs (CBC, LDH). Vaccination and safe sexual practices reduce infection‑related relapses in immunocompromised patients.
b: Every 3–6 months for first 2 years, then annually
Address modifiable risk factors: HIV control, hepatitis treatment

sections.p: Hodgkin lymphoma (presence of Reed‑Sternberg cells, contiguous spread) and reactive lymphadenitis (benign hyperplasia).
b: Hodgkin lymphoma shows CD15/CD30 positivity
Reactive nodes retain normal architecture, lack clonal markers

sections.p: Low LDH does not exclude aggressive disease; small biopsy samples may miss high‑grade areas, leading to under‑staging.
b: False‑negative FISH if tumor cells are sparse
PET‑CT may be falsely negative in low‑grade indolent lymphoma

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden swelling of lymph nodes, high fever, unexplained weight loss, night sweats, or new organ pain

faq.q: Why is CD20 targeted in many NHLs?
faq.a: CD20 is expressed on most B‑cell lymphomas; rituximab binds it, causing cell death and improving outcomes.
Limited‑stage indolent NHL can achieve long‑term remission; aggressive NHL often requires curative intent chemo‑immunotherapy.
